label: Palestinian-Levant
subtitle: Sumac, za'atar, tahini, warm spice
about: Palestinian cooking sits in the eastern Mediterranean Levant, from the Galilee and inland hills to Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza coast, while sharing a wider food region with Lebanon, Syria and Jordan. Centuries of Arab, Ottoman, Mediterranean and trade connections produced related but strongly local traditions; northern Palestine overlaps more with Lebanon, while Gaza is notably hotter and more dill-forward. Representative dishes include musakhan, maqluba, maftoul and Jerusalem ka'ak.
flavors: زعتر (zaʿtar) — the herb and the sesame-sumac-herb blend; formulas vary
دبس الرمان (dibs al-rummān) — pomegranate molasses; more important in some Levantine and northern/regional traditions than others
sweet_only: ماء الورد (māʾ al-ward) — rosewater, used mainly in sweets and desserts
ماء الزهر (māʾ al-zahr) — orange-blossom water, used mainly in sweets, syrups and drinks
signature_ingredients: maftoul — substitute: pearl couscous; LOW CONFIDENCE as a texture substitute because true maftoul is hand-rolled bulgur-and-wheat granules
freekeh — substitute: bulgur; flavor will lack freekeh's characteristic toasted/smoky quality
jameed or dried yogurt — substitute: full-fat Greek yogurt plus a little feta; LOW CONFIDENCE and not equivalent
akkawi or nabulsi-style white cheese — substitute: low-moisture mozzarella mixed with feta; LOW CONFIDENCE and dish-dependent
fresh zaʿatar herb (often Origanum syriacum or related local herbs) — substitute: fresh oregano plus thyme; LOW CONFIDENCE because species and aroma differ
pantry_assumed: No ingredient should be enforced as literally universal. Zaʿatar and olive oil are exceptionally common Palestinian household staples, but availability varies by household and displacement context.
Tahini, sumac, rice, bulgur/freekeh, chickpeas, lentils, yogurt and flatbread are common pantry or refrigerator items across much of the cuisine but should not be hard requirements.
techniques: mahshi: stuffing vegetables or leaves with rice and/or meat
slow simmering of yakhneh-style vegetable-and-meat stews
maqluba method: layering rice, meat and vegetables and inverting the finished pot
roasting or baking meats over bread, as in musakhan, with seasoned onions and olive oil
shortcuts: Commercial zaʿatar: usually a zaʿatar/thyme/oregano/hyssop-type herb plus sumac and sesame; salt and extra spices vary. Substitute 1:1 by weight for a homemade zaʿatar blend. Do not assume salt content; calculate salt grams from the label as sodium mg × 0.0025.

Commercial Arabic baharat or nine-spice: commonly includes some combination of allspice, black pepper, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, cardamom and cumin, but there is no universal Palestinian formula. Substitute 1:1 by weight only when replacing a specified family-style blend; usually salt separately unless the label contains salt. LOW CONFIDENCE for cross-brand equivalence.
allergen_notes: Zaʿatar blends commonly contain sesame; some commercial blends also contain soybean oil, so check labels for soy.
Yogurt, labneh and jameed contain milk.
Pine nuts, walnuts, almonds and pistachios appear frequently as garnishes or fillings; treat the relevant nuts as tree-nut allergens.
Pita, tabun bread, bulgur, freekeh and maftoul contain wheat.
Commercial spice blends vary; do not infer allergen absence from the traditional recipe alone.
pitfalls: Do not use 'Levantine' as permission to erase Palestinian dish identity or silently substitute Lebanese or Syrian versions.
Do not make all Palestinian food uniformly mild: Gazan cooking often uses green or red chile, garlic and dill assertively.
Do not put zaʿatar blend into every dish; the fresh herb and the dried blend are different ingredients.
Do not make hummus, tahini, sumac and pomegranate molasses compulsory in every recipe.
Do not describe maftoul as simply Israeli couscous or pearl couscous; the manufacturing method and texture differ.
Do not treat one family spice mixture as a universal Palestinian 'seven spice' or 'nine spice' formula.
sources: Falastin: A Cookbook, Sami Tamimi and Tara Wigley, 2020

label: Persian
subtitle: Saffron, herbs, dried lime, sour fruit
about: Persian cooking developed across the Iranian plateau between the Caspian Sea, the Zagros and Alborz mountains and the Persian Gulf, with major regional and ethnic variation. Long exchange with Central Asia, the Caucasus, Anatolia, India and the Arab world shaped a cuisine noted for elaborate rice, herbs, sour fruit, nuts and restrained aromatic spices rather than uniform heat. Representative dishes include chelow kabab, ghormeh sabzi, fesenjan and zereshk polo.
flavors: ادویه (adviyeh) — variable spice mixture, not one fixed formula
شنبلیله (šanbalileh) — fenugreek leaf, especially in herb mixtures such as ghormeh sabzi
سماق (somāq) — sumac, especially with kebab and at the table
گلپر (golpar) — Persian hogweed/angelica-family seed powder, used as a condiment in selected dishes
لیمو ترش (limu-ye torš) — fresh sour citrus or lime/lemon juice
sweet_only: گلاب (golāb) — rosewater; mainly associated with sweets, syrups and desserts, although occasional savory uses exist
signature_ingredients: zereshk (barberries) — substitute: unsweetened dried cranberries cut smaller plus a little lemon juice; LOW CONFIDENCE because cranberry is sweeter and less sharply acidic
kashk — substitute: strained full-fat yogurt mixed with a little feta; LOW CONFIDENCE and not equivalent to fermented dried whey
reshteh noodles — substitute: thin egg noodles or linguine broken into shorter lengths; texture differs
sour grapes or verjuice — substitute: diluted lemon juice; LOW CONFIDENCE because aroma differs
Persian-style dried limes — substitute: fresh lime zest plus juice; LOW CONFIDENCE because dried lime has fermented, earthy and bitter notes absent from fresh citrus
pantry_assumed: No pantry item should be enforced as literally universal across Iran.
Rice, onions, turmeric, black pepper, dried herbs, yogurt and souring agents are extremely common in the national Persian repertoire, but regional kitchens differ.
Saffron is culturally central and frequently used for special rice, chicken, sweets and ceremonial cooking, but should not be assumed in every everyday dish.
techniques: parboiling then steaming rice for chelow and polow
forming tahdig deliberately at the bottom of the rice pot
slow simmering khoresh until meat, herbs, legumes or fruit integrate into a concentrated sauce
charcoal or high-heat grilling of kabab
slow cooking sour fruit, nuts or herbs with meat or legumes to create balanced sweet-sour or herbaceous stews
shortcuts: Commercial advieh: formulas vary widely but commonly use cinnamon, cardamom, cumin and/or coriander, sometimes rose petals, dried lime, nutmeg, cloves or black pepper. Substitute 1:1 by weight only for the homemade advieh specified by a recipe. Many commercial versions are salt-free; if salt is present, calculate salt grams from sodium mg × 0.0025. LOW CONFIDENCE for cross-brand flavor equivalence.

Commercial dried-lime powder can replace whole dried lime only approximately. Start around 1-2 g powder for the flavor contribution of one small pierced dried lime and adjust; LOW CONFIDENCE because grind, peel and seed content strongly affect bitterness.

Commercial liquid kashk can replace reconstituted dried kashk by equal finished weight when the recipe specifies prepared kashk; verify salt because brands vary substantially. LOW CONFIDENCE for a universal salt correction.
allergen_notes: Kashk, yogurt, butter and ghee contain milk.
Walnuts are fundamental to fesenjan and other preparations; almonds and pistachios are also common tree nuts in rice and sweets.
Reshteh and most breads contain wheat; some commercial noodles may also contain egg.
Traditional advieh, saffron, turmeric, dried lime and sumac do not inherently require any of the listed major allergens, but commercial blend cross-contact or additives must be checked.
Sesame occurs in some breads and regional preparations but should not be assumed absent from a Persian meal.
pitfalls: Do not make Persian food generically 'Middle Eastern' by defaulting to heavy cumin, coriander and paprika.
Do not make every dish sweet: Persian fruit cookery often uses tartness and controlled sweet-sour balance.
Do not replace dried lime with large amounts of fresh lime and claim equivalence.
Do not treat advieh as one canonical recipe.
Do not skip the rice method: basmati-style rice boiled like ordinary absorption rice will not reproduce classic chelow or polow texture.
Do not add saffron to every dish merely because it is iconic.
Do not treat the Persian national repertoire as identical to every ethnic and regional cuisine within Iran.
sources: Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies, Najmieh Batmanglij, 2011 edition

label: Turkish
subtitle: Pul biber, sumac, yogurt, mint
about: Turkish cuisine spans Anatolia between the Black, Aegean and Mediterranean seas and extends into Turkish Thrace and Istanbul, with major differences among coastal, central, eastern and southeastern regions. It grew from Anatolian regional traditions and centuries of migration and exchange under Seljuk and Ottoman rule, including but not limited to influential palace cooking. Representative foods include kebap, mantı, dolma or sarma, and börek.
flavors: pul biber (pul biber) — crushed red pepper flakes; heat and pepper variety vary
kekik (kekik) — thyme/oregano-type herbs; the Turkish category does not map perfectly to one supermarket species
biber salçası (biber salçası) — red pepper paste, sweet or hot
yenibahar (yenibahar) — allspice, especially in dolma, seasoned rice and some meat dishes
defne yaprağı (defne yaprağı) — bay leaf, especially for fish, meats, tomato dishes and preserves
nar ekşisi (nar ekşisi) — pomegranate reduction; especially characteristic in southern and southeastern regions rather than a nationwide default
sweet_only: gül suyu (gül suyu) — rosewater, mainly in sweets and syrups
damla sakızı (damla sakızı) — mastic, especially in puddings, ice cream and confectionery; regional and not universal
signature_ingredients: yufka — substitute: very thin flour tortillas; LOW CONFIDENCE because elasticity and drying differ
kaymak — substitute: mascarpone loosened with heavy cream; LOW CONFIDENCE because cultured flavor and fat structure differ
sucuk — substitute: a garlic-forward beef sausage; no close typical-US-supermarket equivalent
Turkish erişte — substitute: broad egg noodles; shape and egg content vary
fine and coarse Turkish bulgur grades — substitute: supermarket bulgur of the closest grind; cooking behavior may differ
pantry_assumed: No item should be enforced as literally present in every Turkish household.
Tomato or pepper paste, yogurt, onions, dried mint, pul biber or another red-pepper form, black pepper, rice or bulgur and bread are very common, but regional and household patterns differ.
Nar ekşisi, çemen and tahini should not be treated as universal pantry requirements.
techniques: mangal or ocak grilling for kebap and köfte
slow gentle braising of zeytinyağlı vegetable dishes in olive oil
stuffing and rolling vegetables or leaves for dolma and sarma
layering or rolling yufka and baking or pan-cooking börek
long simmering of soups, legumes and home-style tencere dishes, often finished with butter, pepper, mint or yogurt-based seasoning
shortcuts: Commercial biber salçası: usually concentrated red pepper and salt, sometimes with acidity regulators or preservatives. Replace homemade pepper paste 1:1 by weight. If a brand is 5% salt, 20 g paste contributes about 1.0 g salt; otherwise use the package salt figure rather than assuming 5%.

Commercial Turkish baharat: there is no canonical national formula; products may contain allspice, pepper, cumin, coriander, cinnamon, clove, fennel, mint, paprika or chile. Substitute 1:1 by weight only when replacing a recipe's own mixed spices and verify whether the blend contains salt. LOW CONFIDENCE for universal equivalence.

Commercial nar ekşisi: use 1:1 by weight for pure pomegranate reduction when a recipe calls for nar ekşisi. Products sold as nar ekşili sos may contain sugar, glucose syrup or other ingredients and should not be treated as equivalent. Salt is usually not the principal adjustment; verify the label.
allergen_notes: Yogurt, ayran, butter and many yogurt sauces contain milk.
Tarhana commonly combines fermented grain/flour with yogurt or another dairy component, so it commonly presents both wheat and milk allergens.
Simit usually contains wheat and often sesame, although recognized regional sesame-free simit styles exist.
Börek and yufka contain wheat; fillings may add milk or egg.
Walnuts, pistachios, hazelnuts and almonds occur in regional savory dishes and sweets and are tree-nut allergens.
Simple biber salçası and nar ekşisi formulas do not inherently require the listed major allergens, but commercial sauces and blends must be checked individually.
pitfalls: Do not describe Turkish cuisine as simply Ottoman palace food; palace and folk traditions were distinct and both interacted with many regional cuisines.
Do not use pomegranate molasses in every Turkish salad, kebab or dolma; it is particularly strong in southern and southeastern traditions.
Do not treat fenugreek as a universal Turkish seasoning; its strongest associations are with çemen, pastırma and selected regional dishes.
Do not make every Turkish dish chile-hot; pul biber ranges from mild to hot and many classic dishes are not hot.
Do not assume 'kekik' always means one species of oregano.
Do not make sesame an all-purpose savory seasoning simply because simit is famous.
Do not default every savory recipe to a generic commercial 'Turkish baharat'; tomato paste, pepper paste, herbs, black pepper and regional acids are often more structurally important.
